title: Up-Close: The World’s Most Terrifying Glacier
author: Robert Hunziker
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/dominik-van-
opdenbosch-PtthxYbhYao-
unsplash-1-680x453.jpg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/09/11/up-close-the-
worlds-most-terrifying-glacier/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/dominik-van-
opdenbosch-PtthxYbhYao-unsplash-1-680x453.jpg)

Image by Dominik Van Opdenbosch.

“Thwaites demise is inevitable” (_Inside Antarctica’s Doomsday Glacier_ ,
[PBS,](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YzLra9Yp4FI) August 19th, 2026).

Aboard the South Korean icebreaker _Araon:_ “This is Thwaites, a glacier on
the edge of Earth, teetering on the edge of collapse – the most consequential
glacier on the planet. No ship has ever made it this far. For the scientists
aboard, many of whom have tried and failed to reach this place before, the
anticipation is as palpable as the beauty,” Ibid.

Global warming knows no boundaries, even the most remote where scientists’
boots on the ground tread on the planet’s coldest ecosystem. It’s there that
human-generated global warming undercuts Thwaites Glacier, aka: the Doomsday
Glacier. In time, it’ll collapse. Scientists are trying to discover how and
when, and what to do, if anything.

The Doomsday Glacier epithet is catchy; it sticks in the mind. But is it as
dangerous as it sounds? A recent documented trip aboard the South Korean
icebreaker _Araon_ , operated by the Korea Polar Research Institute, whose
polar research is fully funded through 2031, answers provocative questions and
gives interested parties an up-close look at the monster that rests on a deep
marine bedrock of the Amundsen Sea’s continental shelf in West Antarctica.
There is nothing else that compares to Thwaites. It is uniquely different.

“This is a glacier that is falling apart before our very eyes… when glaciers
go at a certain speed, they just seem to rip apart, and that makes the whole
physics of it overwhelming and difficult.” (David Holland, professor of
mathematics and atmosphere/ocean science at the Courant Institute of
Mathematical Sciences/New York University and a lead Principal Investigator on
the MELT Project, aboard _Araon_)

Of more than passing interests, and of relevance, in October 2025, the U.S.
National Science Foundation (NSF) terminated the lease of the icebreaker
_Nathaniel B. Palmer_ after 33 years of service. It was the United States sole
research icebreaker, providing American polar scientists access to study the
75-mile-wide Thwaites Glacier. The administration’s FY 2027 budget request
proposes a 54% cut to the National Science Foundation plus a 70% cut for
Antarctic research to avoid scaring the living daylights out of American
citizens by exposing the danger of climate change via compulsory reports
required when taxpayer money funds research projects, as well as joining hands
within a tight circle of climate denial right-wing zealots, aka: “the hate
science cabal.” Knowledge is way too challenging to handle.

**Mission to Thwaites**

After a two-week 3,200-mile voyage from Lyttelton, New Zealand _Araon_ reaches
an ideal location at Thwaites Glacier for helicopters to reach the grounding
line where the glacier underwater meets land. The objective is to drill a hole
through the ice and lower instruments into the Amundsen Sea that will remain
in place for one year. “The data might help scientists understand why no
glacier this size on Earth is melting faster and perhaps allow them to predict
when it might collapse,” Ibid.

The scientific mission requires 40 helicopter trips from _Araon_ to a
designated location on Thwaites to set up the equipment to “hot drill” into
the massive glacier. The ice is 3,000 feet thick where the drill team sets up
shop to inject a boiling hot water drill bit into the ice to accomplish two
things: (1) send down instruments for a “snapshot” of conditions below,
including temperature, salinity, and currents (2) the main objective - to send
down similar sensors permanently to transmit data for one year about what’s
happening to cause the glacier to melt so quickly.

The mission requires melting 20 tons of snow for hot water for the drill to
effectively bore through the ice, requiring 23 hours of hard labor shoveling
ice before drilling starts. Then, instruments down the borehole to measure
temperature, depth, water current, and dissolved oxygen and a second time to
permanently measure the underneath side of Thwaites where the glacier meets
groundline.

Oops! An unexpected disaster ensues as the sensitive instruments lowered into
the drill hole freeze solid at 2,300 feet below surface but still several
hundred feet away from the target zone. Antarctica’s impenetrably harsh
conditions sabotage the major objective of the mission. This is years of hard
work dealt a ‘hard blow’ where it hurts most.

Moreover, it’s too late to do more work, out of time, temperatures drop
quickly after summer ends in Antarctica. The sun sets for the last time and
24-hour darkness, the Antarctic Night, sets in. The _Araon_ did not want to
get frozen-in. They had to leave the frozen instruments at 2,300 feet below
surface, frozen for eternity.

However, what was discovered is important as well as concerning. The water
temperature at the bottom of the drill hole was nearly 6.5 degrees warmer than
the freezing point of glacier ice in seawater, irrefutable proof that Thwaites
is rapidly melting from below.

Based upon discussions with David Holland, climate scientist New York
University, who has more than a dozen trips to Antarctica under his belt, not
much solid data on Thwaites exist, but what is known is something mysterious
about the infamous glacier’s behavior requires more in-depth research. It’s
happening too fast.

By permanently placing instruments, scientists hoped to see how underwater
conditions change over time. Alas, it failed. Prior missions to Thwaites to
accomplish this task in 2022 and 2024 found the sea ice so thick that
icebreakers could not reach the glacier. At least the Korean vessel _Araon_
accomplished that. Still, numerous readings and experiments were conducted
throughout the trip even though the prize trophy failed.

**Why Thwaites?**

Won Sang Lee, the lead scientist aboard _Araon_ , explains why South Korea
considers polar research so important: “My country is a peninsula, so facing
everywhere the ocean, so we’re really vulnerable to sea level change.” He
assembled 40 top notch science researchers for the mission.

Thwaites is the one place where warm ocean water abuts the continental shelf
break, flowing to the grounding line. For thousands of years, the continental
shelf itself safe-guarded Thwaites from exposure as a natural underwater dam.
But climate change has altered wind patterns around the Antarctic continent so
that more cold, fresh water near the surface flows out to sea, creating a
pathway for deep warm water to spill over or squeeze over the continental
shelf that previously held it back for thousands of years. Eureka!
Destabilizing Thwaites after tens of thousands of years of relative stability.

**300 Feet (thickness)Lost Annually**

Thwaites is different, according to Dr. Holland: “It is vanishing at an
astonishing rate. It is losing about 300 feet of thickness every year. Whereas
typical melt in Antarctica is less than one foot at the base.”

There are no other glaciers that come close to the singularity of Thwaites,
which is the size of Florida, holding enough ice alone to raise sea levels by
2.5-3 feet. Even more significantly, it is a “keystone” for the West Antarctic
Ice Sheet, holding back the prospect of the entire West Antarctic Ice Sheet
cascading, which would add 10 feet to sea-level rise worldwide. Will this
happen?

If it did add 10 feet, assuming very aggressive estimates, it would take
several decades into 2100 and beyond. However, there are Antarctic polar
scientists who claim, at [polar science
conferences,](https://www.reuters.com/business/environment/scientists-chile-
question-if-antarctica-has-hit-point-no-return-2024-08-28/) 13 feet this
century, which makes 2030-40 look dicey, but far off the mark of mainstream
science. Most climate scientists will scoff at that, maybe giggle or even
laugh out loud. Still, the challenging fact remains that nobody really knows
how much, how soon sea level will become a major nuisance. But it’s coming!

**A Sea Curtain?**

An undersea river valley 60 miles wide funnels the warm water to Thwaites,
melting underneath. Scientists have proposed an underwater barrier or sea
curtain to deflect the warm current from reaching the 60-mile-wide river
valley, hoping to stop or delay Thwaites demise.

The sea curtain idea has some background: “Looking at history, in the First
World War, Britain built anti-submarine nets, curtains, if you like, around
most of its coast, spanning thousands of kilometers… That was a massive
investment at the time, but it was an existential threat, so it had to be
done.” (_Scientists Weigh Giant Sea Curtain to Shield ‘Doomsday Glacier’ From
Melting_ , Mongabay, September 24, 2025)

However, glaciologist Mike Bentley, Durham University/UK wrote a critical
assessment of preserving polar ice: “Safeguarding the Polar Regions from
Dangerous Geoengineering: A Critical Assessment of Proposed Concepts and
Future Prospects,” including an analysis of the sea curtain concept. Alas,
“none of them (five proposals) passed a set of objective criteria on
feasibility, challenges of logistics, scaling-up cost, and governance issues.”
The sea curtain did not escape criticism. Instead, Dr. Bentley suggests
spending the >$100 billion that would be needed for a sea curtain on
decarbonization or adaptation measures.

**Critical “Underwater Current” Issue**

Still hopeful of something positive after the disappointing equipment failure
of the main mission and traveling eighty miles away from Thwaites Glacier at
3,000 feet above the underwater valley that feeds warm water to the grounding
line, the scientists deploy a pair of robotic moorings with sensors that
continuously climb and descend on 1,500-foot cables attached to the seafloor,
recording temperature, salinity, and the speed of the current over the next
year, or two. If the water current is too fast, the sea curtain idea will be
impossible. The two moorings store all data onboard; there is no real-time
data. These robotic moorings will be retrieved within two years to discover
what’s happening and whether a sea curtain is even possible to consider?

The scientific community remains extremely skeptical of sea curtain success
for Thwaites. Still, desperate circumstances require desperate ideas. A sea
curtain to block 60 miles of warm sea water from undercutting Thwaites Glacier
is as desperate as it gets!
